name: humanities
subject: Philosophy of science: Hume and Popper (hand-written fixture)

propositions.name: Induction projects observed regularities
propositions.statement: Inductive inference moves from observed cases (every swan seen so far is white) to a claim about unobserved cases (all swans are white, or the next swan will be white). Unlike a valid deduction, true premises do not guarantee a true conclusion.

propositions.name: Uniformity principle
propositions.statement: Every inductive inference tacitly assumes that unobserved cases resemble observed ones: that the course of nature continues uniformly. Hume identified this assumption as what makes the step from observed to unobserved look reasonable.
aliases: principle of the uniformity of nature

propositions.name: Uniformity cannot be demonstrated
propositions.statement: The denial of the uniformity principle implies no contradiction: we can coherently conceive that the sun will not rise tomorrow. So the principle cannot be established by demonstrative (a priori) reasoning.

propositions.name: Inductive defence of induction is circular
propositions.statement: Arguing that the uniformity principle is true because it has held in the past is itself an inductive inference, so it presupposes the very principle it is meant to support.

propositions.name: Hume's problem of induction
propositions.statement: Because the uniformity principle can be justified neither demonstratively nor inductively, Hume concluded that inductive inference has no rational justification. We expect regularities to continue from custom or habit, not from reason.

propositions.name: Verification-falsification asymmetry
propositions.statement: No finite number of observed white swans can prove "all swans are white", but one genuine black swan refutes it by modus tollens. Universal claims can be falsified deductively but never verified.

propositions.name: Popper's falsificationism
propositions.statement: Popper held that science does not need induction: scientists propose bold conjectures and try to refute them by deductive tests. A theory is scientific only if it forbids some possible observations, that is, if it is falsifiable.

propositions.name: Corroboration is not confirmation
propositions.statement: For Popper, a theory that survives severe tests is corroborated. Corroboration reports how the theory has performed so far; it does not make the theory more probably true or give a reason to expect it to keep passing.

propositions.name: Demarcation by falsifiability
propositions.statement: Popper used falsifiability to separate science from non-science, not meaningful from meaningless. He judged Freud's and Adler's psychology unscientific because any behaviour could be explained by them, unlike Einstein's 1919 light-bending prediction, which could have failed.

arguments.message:
## What induction is

You've seen the sun rise every morning of your life, so you expect it tomorrow. That step, from cases you've observed to cases you haven't, is **induction**.

Compare it with deduction. In a valid deduction, if the premises are true the conclusion can't be false. Induction gives no such guarantee: every swan Europeans had seen was white, and then black swans turned up in Australia.

Hume asked what licenses the step. His answer: every inductive inference relies on an unstated assumption, that the unobserved will resemble the observed. Call it the **uniformity principle**. Without it, 'the sun has always risen' gives no reason at all to expect tomorrow's sunrise.

So the question becomes: what justifies the uniformity principle?

## Hume's dilemma

Hume splits reasoning into two kinds: **demonstrative** reasoning about relations of ideas (maths, logic) and **probable** reasoning about matters of fact. Try to justify the uniformity principle with each.

1. **Demonstratively?** A demonstrative truth is one whose denial is a contradiction. But 'the sun will not rise tomorrow' is perfectly conceivable, no more contradictory than 'it will rise'. So no a priori proof is available.
2. **Probably?** You might say: nature has always been uniform before, so it will be uniform again. But that argument is itself inductive. It assumes the principle in order to prove it, which is circular.

Both routes fail, so Hume concludes that our inductive expectations have no rational foundation. We form them anyway, out of **custom or habit**: repeated experience trains the mind to expect the usual. That is a fact about human psychology, not a justification.

## Popper's way out

Popper accepted Hume's argument completely and drew a radical conclusion: science doesn't use induction at all.

The key is an asymmetry. A million white swans don't prove 'all swans are white'. One black swan disproves it, by plain deduction (modus tollens: if all swans are white, this swan is white; this swan is not white; so not all swans are white).

So, Popper says, science proceeds by **conjectures and refutations**: propose a bold theory, deduce what it forbids, and look hard for exactly that. A theory that survives isn't shown true. It is **corroborated**, which is only a report of how it has done under test so far. Popper is careful here: corroboration doesn't make a theory more probable, otherwise he'd be smuggling induction back in.

## Drawing the line

Popper's other use of falsifiability was the **demarcation problem**: what separates science from non-science? (Not from nonsense. Popper thought non-scientific ideas could be meaningful and even true.)

His examples came from Vienna around 1919. Freud's and Adler's theories seemed to be confirmed by everything: a man who pushes a child into water and a man who saves a drowning child could both be explained. That, Popper said, is the weakness. A theory compatible with every possible observation tells us nothing.

Einstein was different. General relativity predicted that starlight would bend by a definite amount near the sun, and Eddington's 1919 eclipse expedition could have shown it didn't. The theory took a real risk. That risk is the mark of science.
